_doc: Surname plus a compatible forename over every person in data/residents/households/. A WORKLIST, not a merge list: the ruling for each cluster is in merge_rulings.json and the merge itself is landed by tools/merge_resident_cards.py --apply.

links.rule: an initial reaching a full name
an initial reaching a full name

against: the cards state different trades: clerk, merchant, none_recorded
not every card's person is a head: head, son
one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: andreas_1884_v1 -> wright_john, wright_john_s

clusters.why: A FATHER AND HIS SON, and they already stand on one card. Andreas names John Wright, merchant, and John S. Wright, clerk, his son — `hh_wright_john` carries both, the second with relationship `son`. Folding them would delete a person the sources explicitly count. `wright_j`, the American's bare `J Wright` of July 1835, could be either of them or a third Wright (Amasa, Robert C. and Truman G. also stand in the town), and no source reached decides it — that one is UNDECIDED and goes to the owner rather than to a guess.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: boarding_house_keeper
against: the cards state different sexes: female, male
not every card's person is a head: head, wife
one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: andreas_1884_v1 -> brown_rufus, brown_mrs_rufus

clusters.why: TWO PEOPLE, not one card split — the opposite fault. `Mrs Rufus Brown` is a woman (sex female, relationship wife) whom the honorific strip folded onto her husband's forename, so the candidate pass sees `Rufus` on both. Andreas names the Green Tree tavern's keeper and his wife. They must not be merged. This pair is T-0723's — 'One identity, two town cards' — and that ticket is IN FLIGHT on another branch as this ruling is written. The reading is recorded here so the sweep is complete and no later pass re-asks; the CARDS are deliberately not touched, because two runs writing the same two records is how a merge queue loses work.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: none_recorded

clusters.why: OWNER. Two thin readings and NO anchor: `John A Clark` is the Democrat of 11 February 1834 and `John K Clark` the American of 11 July 1835, each a single printing, neither carrying a trade, a seat or a biographical source. They agree on John and disagree on the middle letter. Where an anchor stands behind one card this pass folds the thin readings onto it; here there is nothing to fold onto, and picking one of two equal readings would invent the man it kept. Erastus and Timothy J. Clark are outside this cluster.

links.rule: an initial reaching a full name

against: the cards state different trades: none_recorded, ship_carpenter

clusters.why: ONE MAN ON TWO CARDS, and the merge is right: `N. R. Norton` is Nelson R. Norton, the ship carpenter Andreas names, carried a second time from a letter list. The middle initial agrees and the town holds no second N. Norton. But this is the second of T-0723's two named cases. This pair is T-0723's — 'One identity, two town cards' — and that ticket is IN FLIGHT on another branch as this ruling is written. The reading is recorded here so the sweep is complete and no later pass re-asks; the CARDS are deliberately not touched, because two runs writing the same two records is how a merge queue loses work.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: none_recorded
against: one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: chicago_democrat_1833_1835 -> saunders_william_s, saunders_william_w

clusters.why: OWNER. `William S. Saunders` is a letter-list-only card; `William W Saunders` is a single Democrat printing of March 1834. Same paper, same forename, contradicted middle letter, no anchor behind either and no trade, seat or date to test. The town holds no third Saunders to break the tie.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: none_recorded
against: one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: chicago_voter_lists_1833_1835_irad -> smith_william, smith_william_v

clusters.why: Two men, not one. Both cards are ATTESTED at G1a with independent multi-source identities — William Smith on the Black Hawk enrolments, the 1840 census and both directories; William V. Smith on the Democrat and the voter lists — and the SAME 1833-1835 voter roll prints both, which is a roll naming each elector once. Smith is the commonest surname in the corpus and William the commonest forename; folding them on a bare initial would be the exact error name_agreement.py was written to stop.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: none_recorded
against: one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: chicago_democrat_1833_1835 -> taylor_william, taylor_william_h

clusters.why: OWNER. `William Taylor` and `William H Taylor` are two Democrat printings ten months apart, neither with a trade, a seat or a biographical source. Nothing CONTRADICTS — the bare card simply says less — so this is not a refusal; but Taylor is one of the town's crowded surnames (Anson, Augustine Deodat, Charles H., E. D. all stand on their own cards) and no anchor decides whether the bare reading is the same man. The owner's call.

for: the trade agrees on every card that states one: none_recorded
against: one source prints more than one of these cards, which is a source naming two people on one page unless the printings are the same line: chicago_democrat_1833_1835 -> walker_george_e, walker_george_h

clusters.why: OWNER. `George E. Walker` is a letter-list card the Fergus 1843 death notices also reach; `George H Walker` is the Black Hawk enrolments and the Democrat at G1c. The middle letters contradict, both cards carry real independent evidence, and neither is anchored in a biographical source that would settle which letter the man used. James and Jeremiah Walker are outside this cluster.
